question: Can a forecasting Transformer represent sample-dependent, non-affine changes in effective temporal pace more faithfully than fixed-index positional encodings by learning a monotone clock and using it to drive stable two-dimensional Hamiltonian attention flows?

key_findings.claim: The paper proves a narrow exact-representation obstruction for a single fixed RoPE frequency, not an impossibility result for an entire content-aware Transformer.
key_findings.evidence: Theorem 3.1 shows that, under a non-aliasing condition, no constant angular frequency theta can satisfy theta(m-n) = omega_0[tau(m)-tau(n)] modulo 2 pi for every pair when tau is non-affine. The proof only concerns the positional phase identity. Queries, keys, multiple frequency bands, absolute embeddings, MLPs, and content-dependent attention remain available to a standard Transformer, so later prose saying RoPE-based models are mathematically incapable of synchronizing with non-affine dynamics is stronger than the theorem.

key_findings.claim: SyPE couples a learned monotone clock to stable anisotropic two-dimensional Hamiltonian flows, but the implemented family is a stability-constrained subset rather than the unrestricted symplectic group.
key_findings.evidence: Each local increment is Softplus(w_tau^T h_t), and cumulative sums form the warped coordinate. For every paired head dimension, a symmetric K with det(K)>0 generates S(t)=exp(tJK); queries use S(tau_m), keys use J S(tau_n), and the symplectic identity reduces the score to a function of tau_n-tau_m. Appendix A parameterizes a=exp(alpha), b=exp(beta), c=tanh(gamma)sqrt(ab), forcing oscillatory eigenvalues and excluding hyperbolic or parabolic symplectic flows. This design can dilate or contract a forward clock but cannot reverse it.

key_findings.claim: On the controlled warped seasonal process, StretchTime improves most strongly at long horizons and the geometry-plus-clock variant beats both fixed RoPE and a no-MLP ablation.
key_findings.evidence: At horizons 96, 192, 336, and 720, StretchTime reports MSE/MAE of 0.053/0.180, 0.073/0.207, 0.120/0.255, and 0.331/0.416. RoPE reports 0.058/0.186, 0.084/0.219, 0.184/0.311, and 0.411/0.480; the no-MLP variant reports 0.078/0.218, 0.105/0.250, 0.161/0.298, and 0.358/0.439. Average MSE is 0.144 versus 0.184 and 0.176. The paper does not report recovered-clock error, repeated-seed uncertainty, or the numerical generator parameters A, P, phi, omega_0, and sigma, so the experiment validates forecasting on one described warp family rather than recovery of its latent clock.

key_findings.claim: StretchTime is consistently better than its matched RoPE backbone, but it is not the lowest-error method on most real datasets.
key_findings.evidence: Dataset-averaged MSE improves over RoPE on all ten reported datasets: Weather 0.237 versus 0.244, Solar 0.195 versus 0.214, ECL 0.174 versus 0.179, ETTh1 0.424 versus 0.449, ETTh2 0.384 versus 0.401, ETTm1 0.367 versus 0.379, ETTm2 0.276 versus 0.287, PEMS03 0.094 versus 0.107, PEMS04 0.088 versus 0.090, and PEMS08 0.118 versus 0.125. It ranks first on only four of ten datasets; TimeMixer++ is better on Weather, ETTh1, ETTh2, and ETTm2, OLinear is better on ECL, ETTh2, ETTm2, and PEMS08, and the PEMS04 gain over RoPE is only 0.002 MSE.

key_findings.claim: The headline 'best overall' ranking depends on aggregation: StretchTime wins after averaging each dataset first, while OLinear wins when every dataset-horizon cell is ranked.
key_findings.evidence: Main Table 2 reports dataset-level average ranks of 2.20 for StretchTime, 2.30 for OLinear, and 2.80 for TimeMixer++, supporting the headline. Appendix Table 5 instead ranks all horizon-level MSE cells and reports 2.27 for StretchTime, 2.08 for OLinear, and 3.17 for TimeMixer++; TimeMixer++ has 17 first-place cells, StretchTime 13, and OLinear 12. Neither aggregation is inherently invalid, but the paper does not disclose this winner reversal in its main claim.

key_findings.claim: The adaptive clock has clearer ablation support than the symplectic geometry itself.
key_findings.evidence: Across the five datasets in Table 4, full StretchTime and the rotation-only 'w/o Symplectic' variant both average 0.338 MSE, while fixing the clock raises the average to 0.341. The full model is only 0.001 better on Weather and 0.004 on ETTm2, ties on ETTh2 and ETTm1, and is 0.003 worse on ETTh1. Thus the table supports a small benefit from learned warping and mixed, near-zero average evidence for anisotropic symplectic degrees of freedom, contrary to prose that treats the comparison as validation of the full geometry.

key_findings.claim: A broader matched-backbone appendix comparison strongly favors the complete SyPE-plus-warp module over static attention alternatives, while still not isolating geometry from warping.
key_findings.evidence: Across 40 dataset-horizon MSE cells, StretchTime has average rank 1.05 and is best in 38; RoPE has 2.73 and one win, Pure Softmax 2.65 and no wins, and Linear Attention plus RoPE 3.50 and one win. The two exceptions are PEMS04 at horizon 24, where RoPE gives 0.079 versus 0.081, and PEMS04 at horizon 96, where Linear Attention plus RoPE gives 0.109 versus 0.112. Because this table compares the complete module with alternatives, it cannot overturn Table 4's weak evidence for the symplectic-only increment.

key_findings.claim: The reported resource advantage is substantial against large Transformer baselines but is not an end-to-end deployment comparison.
key_findings.evidence: On ETTm1, StretchTime averages 2.79 GFLOPs and 493.75K parameters over four horizons, versus 6.25 GFLOPs and 1.22M parameters for TimeMixer++, 2.85 GFLOPs and 1.17M for TimeMixer, roughly 212.75M FLOPs and 9.68M parameters for iTransformer, and 2.54 GFLOPs and 11.53M parameters for PatchTST. DLinear is far smaller at 905.25K FLOPs and 65.25K parameters but has worse average MSE, 0.404 versus 0.367. No training time, inference latency, peak memory, learned-clock overhead, or hardware-normalized throughput is reported.

key_findings.claim: Several internal reporting and reproducibility contradictions materially narrow the strength of the empirical conclusion.
key_findings.evidence: Section 4.2 says twelve benchmarks and 'four PEMS datasets' while naming only PEMS03, PEMS04, and PEMS08; Table 2 contains ten datasets; Appendix C.1 says eight but describes ten; Appendix E says nine while Table 6 again contains ten. The paper calls the baseline comparison strictly fair, yet Appendix C.1 says TimeMixer++ numbers were copied from its paper because the official code could not be reproduced, and OLinear values were also sourced externally. All training uses only seed 2026, with no error bars or significance tests.

anchors.section: C.1 baseline sourcing and exclusions / C.2 seed

key_findings.claim: Appendix A establishes symplectic conservation and a closed-form stable flow, but its claimed exact reduction to RoPE is incomplete as written.
key_findings.evidence: For K=omega I, S(t) becomes the usual two-dimensional rotation. Standard RoPE scores arbitrary projected vectors as q^T R(delta)k, whereas the SyPE score retained by the paper is q^T J R(delta)k. Appendix A.2 demonstrates cosine recovery only for a chosen pair of basis vectors; it does not provide an equality for arbitrary q and k or explicitly absorb J into the learned key projection. Functional inclusion is plausible because a fixed J can be folded into W_K, but the printed derivation does not prove the stated exact recovery on its own.

method.core_idea: Replace a fixed index clock in rotary attention with a sample-dependent cumulative clock, and replace isotropic rotations with stable anisotropic Hamiltonian flows so attention can rescale local temporal phase while retaining a relative-coordinate form.
method.mechanism: For each target channel, StretchTime forms tokens from a projected all-channel context, a channel-specific scalar-value basis, a learnable absolute position, and a channel ID. Hidden states produce positive local clock increments through Softplus, whose cumulative sum is monotone. Each pair of head coordinates has a learned positive-definite symmetric Hamiltonian K; the closed-form flow S(t)=cos(omega t)I+sin(omega t)JK/omega transforms the query, while J S(t) transforms the key, making the bilinear score depend on the learned relative clock difference. Three pre-norm Transformer layers forecast last-value-centered increments, restore the last observed value, and use random-ratio channel dropout during training.
assumptions: The useful temporal deformation is monotone, so effective time can slow down or speed up but never reverse.
Local positive increments inferred from hidden content are identifiable from forecasting loss without direct clock supervision.
A collection of stable two-dimensional Hamiltonian flows is an adequate approximation to the relevant temporal geometry.
Anisotropic query-key transformations remain numerically conditioned even though det(K)>0 alone does not bound the condition number of K or S(t).
Known regular sampling indices can stand in for physical time on the real benchmarks; explicit irregular timestamps are not supplied.
Last-value residualization, channel-value tokenization, absolute embeddings, channel dropout, and the SyPE module can be cleanly separated by the reported ablations.
MSE on the standard fixed splits is an informative proxy for phase fidelity and non-stationary temporal robustness.
Cross-paper baseline numbers remain comparable under the stated common benchmark protocol even when an official implementation cannot be reproduced.

techniques.role: Turns content-dependent positive local increments into sample- and channel-conditioned temporal coordinates.
Uses stable Hamiltonian matrix exponentials in paired head dimensions to modulate relative-time attention.
Enforces oscillatory rather than divergent flows through exponential diagonal terms and a tanh-bounded cross term.
Evaluates each two-dimensional flow with sine and cosine instead of a generic matrix exponential.
Combines global multivariate context with channel-specific scalar values, channel IDs, and absolute positions.
Centers every input window at its final observation and predicts increments before adding the level back.
Drops a sample-dependent fraction of channels and rescales survivors to discourage brittle channel dependence.
Creates a controlled oscillating clock in a seasonal AR(1) process to stress fixed-frequency phase tracking.
Pairs query and key through J so symplectic conservation yields dependence on the difference of learned clocks.

limitations: Author-stated: StretchTime has not been scaled to massive pretraining datasets or tested as a zero-shot forecasting foundation model.
Author-stated: the symplectic warping framework is untested outside time series, including natural language and other general sequence tasks.
Author-stated: Traffic and PEMS07 are excluded because TimeMixer exceeded memory available on an RTX 4090, so the traffic comparison is incomplete.

Author-stated: Exchange is excluded because the authors regard its random-walk behavior and strong last-value baseline as uninformative, which removes a difficult negative-control regime from the main panel.

Author-stated: TimeMixer++ results could not be reproduced with its official code and, together with OLinear, are copied from the original papers despite the text describing the comparison as strictly fair.
Reviewer-identified: all experiments use one seed, with no repeated-run variance, confidence intervals, paired tests, or correction for selecting among many dataset-horizon cells.

Reviewer-identified: the synthetic generator does not report enough numerical parameters or split details to reconstruct the claimed phase-warp stress test, and it never measures whether the learned clock recovers the known tau.

Reviewer-identified: outperforming fixed RoPE on naturally non-stationary datasets does not identify time warping as the causal data property; no timestamp warp annotation, learned-clock diagnostic, or counterfactual de-warping test is provided.

Reviewer-identified: Table 4 gives the full symplectic model and rotation-only learned-clock model the same average MSE, so the evidence is mainly for adaptive timing rather than Hamiltonian anisotropy.

Reviewer-identified: the main average-rank SOTA claim is aggregation-sensitive and reverses in Appendix Table 5, where OLinear has the better horizon-level rank and TimeMixer++ has more first-place cells.

Reviewer-identified: theorem statements concern exact positional phase or heavily simplified position-only predictors, not the approximation capacity of complete Transformers with content paths, multiple frequencies, absolute embeddings, and MLPs.

Reviewer-identified: Appendix B's shared-APE impossibility assumes prediction from position alone, whereas the evaluated models condition on observed values and the proposed model itself adds shared absolute embeddings; the proposition therefore does not establish a general APE limitation.

Reviewer-identified: the stability constraint ensures imaginary eigenvalues but does not bound anisotropic conditioning; extreme a/b ratios can amplify coordinates despite non-divergent temporal eigenvalues.

Reviewer-identified: the model combines last-value residualization, mixed channel tokens, channel dropout, absolute embeddings, adaptive warping, and symplectic scoring; the reported ablations do not fully factorialize these choices.

Reviewer-identified: dataset counts conflict across the main text and appendices, and exact split files, code revision, training epochs, and an implementation repository for StretchTime are not supplied in the paper.
Reviewer-identified: parameter and FLOP tables omit wall-clock latency, peak memory, training cost, and clock/flow kernel overhead, so resource-constrained deployment remains an extrapolation.
failure_modes: A non-monotone process, phase reset, or event that requires time reversal cannot be represented by cumulative positive Softplus increments.

When input content is noisy, local clock increments can jitter and create spurious phase dilation; the ETTh1 ablation already shows the more flexible geometry can underperform rotation-only attention.
Extreme Hamiltonian anisotropy can yield poorly conditioned query-key coordinates even when det(K)>0 keeps eigenvalues oscillatory.
A globally shared or weakly identified clock can conflate amplitude, trend, regime shift, and actual temporal pace, producing an appealing but non-causal warp explanation.
MSE training can reward smoothed forecasts and good level tracking without accurate peak timing, particularly when phase error is not evaluated separately.
Irregularly sampled data with real timestamp gaps may require observed continuous time; index-conditioned hidden clocks can mistake missingness or sampling policy for system dynamics.
Purely stochastic or near-random-walk series provide little periodic structure for SyPE to exploit and may favor simpler last-value or linear models.
Channel dropout can damage sparse systems in which a small set of channels carries indispensable causal information.
Very long extrapolation can accumulate small positive-increment errors into large clock drift because no explicit long-horizon clock calibration is imposed.
Cross-domain or zero-shot use may fail because the learned Hamiltonians and warp network are dataset-specific rather than tied to physical timestamps or invariant units.
reusable_insights: Separate the question of where a model attends from the coordinate system in which relative distance is measured; a learned monotone clock is a lightweight way to make that coordinate content-dependent.
When a geometric generalization and an adaptive controller are introduced together, include a rotation-only adaptive-controller baseline because the controller may explain nearly all gains.
Use known-warp synthetic data to measure latent clock recovery and forecast phase error directly, not only aggregate MSE.
Stable low-dimensional matrix flows can be evaluated in closed form, retaining structured inductive bias without generic matrix-exponential overhead.
Rank claims should be reported under both per-dataset and per-task aggregation when datasets contain unequal numbers or scales of horizons.
Exact representation theorems about positional modules should not be promoted to whole-network impossibility claims unless content pathways and approximation are controlled.
A negative-control regime with little forecastable temporal structure is useful for testing whether an adaptive temporal module learns genuine clocks or merely additional capacity.
Source all baselines through a shared executable harness or label cross-paper values separately from reproduced matched baselines.
open_questions: Does the learned cumulative clock correlate with the known tau on synthetic data, and is it identifiable up to affine rescaling across seeds?
Would a learned clock plus ordinary RoPE match the full model on all ten datasets under repeated, power-calibrated runs?
Can a bounded-condition Hamiltonian parameterization preserve anisotropy without amplifying attention logits?
How does StretchTime compare directly with continuous-time positional embeddings, Time2Vec, DILATE, adaptive tokenization, and neural time-warping methods under the same splits?
Do real PEMS and Solar gains persist after controlling for calendar covariates, daylight duration, missingness, and explicit timestamps?
Can a phase-sensitive metric or peak-time error demonstrate improvement that is hidden or confounded in MSE and MAE?
What happens under abrupt phase resets, non-monotone event time, irregular sampling, and regime changes outside the training range?
Does a shared clock, a per-channel clock, or a low-rank family of clocks offer the best accuracy-identifiability tradeoff?
Is the J factor in the SyPE score explicitly absorbable into the implemented key projection, and can the authors provide a full arbitrary-vector RoPE reduction?
Will the dataset-level SOTA conclusion survive a preregistered multi-seed comparison against OLinear, TimeMixer++, STAEformer, CTLPE, and BSAT in one codebase?

competitive_landscape.title: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational positional-mechanism prior and the matched internal baseline generalized by StretchTime.
competitive_landscape.difference: RoFormer uses fixed orthogonal rotations to encode absolute positions while exposing relative offsets in attention. StretchTime replaces index offsets with a learned monotone clock and uses anisotropic Hamiltonian flows; its theorem excludes exact fixed-phase matching for a prescribed non-affine warp but does not show a full RoFormer network cannot approximate the task.

competitive_landscape.title: Time2Vec: Learning a Vector Representation of Time
competitive_landscape.relationship: Early learnable temporal-representation prior omitted from the target's related work.
competitive_landscape.difference: Time2Vec adds model-agnostic learned linear and periodic coordinates for synchronous or asynchronous time. StretchTime instead infers a sample-dependent cumulative pace from hidden content and injects it into relative attention; it should be compared to Time2Vec to determine whether Hamiltonian scoring adds value beyond learned periodic features.

competitive_landscape.title: Shape and Time Distortion Loss for Training Deep Time Series Forecasting Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct forecasting prior for differentiable temporal distortion under non-stationarity.
competitive_landscape.difference: DILATE incorporates shape and differentiable time-distortion penalties into the training loss and evaluates non-stationary multi-step forecasts across backbone classes. StretchTime keeps MSE and changes attention coordinates; it neither compares with a temporal-distortion objective nor reports the phase-sensitive metrics DILATE motivates.

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Time Warping For Multiple Sequence Alignment
competitive_landscape.relationship: Learnable monotone-warp mechanism prior in time-series alignment.
competitive_landscape.difference: Neural Time Warping continuously relaxes discrete multiple-sequence alignment and guarantees a feasible alignment under mild conditions. StretchTime learns an implicit per-sample clock only through forecasting loss and does not align sequences or supervise tau; its novelty lies in coupling a warp to attention rather than introducing neural time warping itself.

competitive_landscape.title: Continuous-Time Linear Positional Embedding for Irregular Time Series Forecasting
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest positional-encoding prior for non-uniform physical time in forecasting.
competitive_landscape.difference: CTLPE encodes observed irregular timestamps through a learned continuous linear function and compares against neural-CDE positional embeddings. StretchTime operates on regular benchmark indices and infers latent pace from content, addressing endogenous warping rather than measured gaps; the target does not test CTLPE or irregular sampling.

competitive_landscape.title: STAEformer: Spatio-Temporal Adaptive Embedding Makes Vanilla Transformer SOTA for Traffic Forecasting
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct adaptive-embedding competitor on the PEMS traffic regime where StretchTime reports its clearest wins.
competitive_landscape.difference: STAEformer learns adaptive spatial-temporal embeddings and chronological information on five traffic datasets. StretchTime uses a general multivariate tokenization and latent monotone clock, but omits STAEformer from PEMS comparisons, so its traffic superiority is not established against the most task-specific adaptive-embedding prior.

competitive_landscape.title: BSAT: B-Spline Adaptive Tokenizer for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
competitive_landscape.relationship: Immediate pre-target adaptive-time and learnable-RoPE competitor omitted from the paper.
competitive_landscape.difference: BSAT places variable-length tokens at high-curvature regions with B-splines and combines learnable absolute embeddings with layer-wise learnable-base RoPE. It adapts sampling resolution rather than learning a cumulative clock and emphasizes compression, but it predates StretchTime by five weeks and directly weakens any broad claim that adaptive temporal coordinates or learnable rotary frequency are new.

competitive_landscape.title: Non-stationary Transformers: Exploring the Stationarity in Time Series Forecasting
competitive_landscape.difference: Non-stationary Transformers combines series stationarization with content-conditioned de-stationary attention and reports large gains for several Transformer backbones. StretchTime targets varying temporal pace through positional geometry, but does not compare against this alternative explanation and intervention for the same broad non-stationarity claim.

competitive_landscape.title: TimesNet: Temporal 2D-Variation Modeling for General Time Series Analysis
competitive_landscape.relationship: Adaptive multi-periodicity baseline included in the target's main tables.
competitive_landscape.difference: TimesNet discovers multiple periods with Fourier analysis and models intra- and inter-period variation as two-dimensional tensors across five tasks. StretchTime instead learns local pace continuously inside attention and is much smaller in the reported ETTm1 comparison, but only evaluates forecasting and does not directly verify recovered periods.

competitive_landscape.title: Multi-resolution Time-Series Transformer for Long-term Forecasting
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct positional and multi-period forecasting prior omitted from the comparison.
competitive_landscape.difference: MTST uses multiple patch resolutions and relative positional encoding to capture localized high-frequency behavior and long seasonal structure simultaneously. StretchTime keeps point-level tokens and adjusts a learned clock; no matched test separates adaptive phase from the established multi-resolution route to varying periodicity.

competitive_landscape.title: A Time Series is Worth 64 Words: Long-term Forecasting with Transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Established channel-independent Transformer baseline used for accuracy and parameter claims.
competitive_landscape.difference: PatchTST tokenizes fixed-length subseries and shares a Transformer across channels, reducing attention cost and extending context. StretchTime uses channel-value mixed point tokens and a learned clock; its reported 0.494M versus roughly 11.5M parameter advantage on ETTm1 is not accompanied by matched latency or tuning-budget analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: iTransformer: Inverted Transformers Are Effective for Time Series Forecasting
competitive_landscape.relationship: Established variate-token Transformer baseline used for accuracy and efficiency claims.
competitive_landscape.difference: iTransformer inverts tokenization so attention models cross-variate correlations and MLPs model each series' temporal trace. StretchTime retains temporal tokens with explicit channel context and learned warped positions; its lower parameter count comes with a different tokenization and no equal-capacity comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: TimeMixer++: A General Time Series Pattern Machine for Universal Predictive Analysis
competitive_landscape.relationship: Strongest broad baseline by dataset wins and the closest reported accuracy-efficiency comparator.
competitive_landscape.difference: TimeMixer++ mixes multi-scale time and multi-resolution frequency images across eight analysis tasks. It beats StretchTime on four dataset averages and has 17 versus 13 horizon-level wins, while StretchTime reports about 55% fewer ETTm1 FLOPs. Because the authors could not reproduce its official code and copied its results, neither accuracy nor efficiency is a fully matched comparison.

competitive_landscape.title: OLinear: A Linear Model for Time Series Forecasting in Orthogonally Transformed Domain
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct linear competitor and alternate winner under the appendix's horizon-level aggregation.
competitive_landscape.difference: OLinear decorrelates temporal features with a data-adaptive orthogonal transform and uses normalized linear multivariate mixing across 24 benchmarks. It obtains horizon-level average rank 2.08 versus StretchTime's 2.27 and is better on several less-periodic datasets, challenging a blanket need for attention or symplectic geometry; its numbers were not rerun in the target harness.

competitive_landscape.title: Linear Transformers as VAR Models: Aligning Autoregressive Attention Mechanisms with Autoregressive Forecasting
competitive_landscape.relationship: Architecture-alignment competitor represented only by an appendix linear-attention ablation.
competitive_landscape.difference: SAMoVAR rearranges linear attention, MLPs, and information flow so multilayer attention retains an interpretable dynamic VAR structure. StretchTime's appendix shows its full softmax SyPE model beating a generic Linear Attention plus RoPE variant, but it does not compare against SAMoVAR's structurally aligned implementation or isolate positional warping from autoregressive alignment.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper claims to formalize non-affine temporal stretching, prove that fixed RoPE cannot represent it, introduce Symplectic Positional Embeddings as a strict Hamiltonian generalization of RoPE with an input-dependent warp module, and achieve state-of-the-art multivariate forecasting with high efficiency.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The pinned v1 contains an exact fixed-frequency phase obstruction, a symplectic conservation derivation and closed-form flow, one warped seasonal synthetic task, ten real benchmark tables, matched RoPE and attention ablations, a limited geometry-versus-clock ablation, and parameter/FLOP accounting.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is the particular composition of a content-conditioned monotone cumulative clock, a J-paired relative attention score, and stability-constrained anisotropic two-dimensional Hamiltonian flows inside a compact forecasting Transformer. Learned temporal vectors, neural time warping, differentiable time-distortion losses, continuous-time positional encodings, adaptive traffic embeddings, non-stationary attention, learned rotary frequencies, and adaptive temporal tokenization all predate it. The main causal contribution is further narrowed because the rotation-only learned-clock variant ties the full geometry on average, the RoPE theorem is only an exact phase statement, and the SOTA winner changes with aggregation. The work is therefore a promising structured attention design with strong matched-RoPE evidence, not yet a general proof that symplectic geometry is necessary or that real benchmark gains arise from latent time warping.

reviewer_notes: Read the pinned 17-page v1 end to end, including Appendices A-F, and checked the rendered equations and Tables 1-6 against the extracted text. Physical PDF pages equal the printed page numbers. The official record was checked on 2026-08-23: arXiv:2602.08983v1, submitted 2026-02-09, remains the current and only revision. An explicit https://export.arxiv.org/pdf/2602.08983v1 download was byte-identical to the indexed PDF SHA-256. Primary-source searches covered three families: mechanism plus task ('learned time warping positional encoding forecasting'), evaluation plus closest baseline ('multivariate forecasting RoPE adaptive periodicity PEMS'), and novelty plus cited predecessor ('symplectic attention continuous-time embedding adaptive tokenizer'), followed by a current-through-2026 scan. Fifteen exact arXiv revisions were checked. Author results, reviewer inference, negative results, and contradiction audits are separated. No second-reviewer verification is claimed.
